1:
The second round of the controversy opens here, and the voices agree on who opens it. Gill makes Eliphaz the first of Job's friends and comforters, the oldest of them, whose turn it is to answer a second time; Keil and Delitzsch call him the most respectable and most influential of the three, and read Job's long and bitter answers as seeming to him empty words and impassioned tirades that ill become a wise man such as he claims to be. Their rendering sharpens the opening question into whether a wise man utters vain knowledge and fills his breast with the east wind. Clarke would put it as the science of wind, a science without solidity or certainty, and his note on the east wind is the fullest: a very stormy wind in the Levant, supposed to be the euroclydon of the Greeks, so that Eliphaz means Job's speech to have been a perfect storm or tempest of words. Wesley adds that such discourse is not merely unprofitable but pernicious, as that wind was in those parts.

Henry is the one voice that turns first on the speaker rather than the speech. Eliphaz falls very foul upon Job because Job contradicted the friends and did not applaud them as they expected, and proud people are apt to take it amiss if they may not dictate and give law to all about them, censuring as ignorant and obstinate everyone who cannot say as they say. Representing an adversary's reasoning as ridiculous is the common habit of angry disputants, who forget the doom of him that calls his brother a fool. Having said that, Henry grants the general truths the charge is built on: that there is in the world a great deal of vain knowledge, falsely so called, which puffs men up with a fond conceit of their own accomplishments, and that unprofitable talk is evil talk, since we must account in the great day not only for wicked words but for idle ones.

On the heavier charge, that Job has cast off fear and restrained prayer, Henry pauses over what it assumes: that religion is summed up in fearing God and praying to him, the former the most needful principle and the latter the most needful practice, so that the prayerless are fearless and graceless. The others locate the fault in the consequences of Job's doctrine rather than in his practice. Ellicott holds that Job's tendency has been to encourage a kind of fatalism and so to check the offering of prayer, besides setting an example which from his position was likely to be followed into murmuring. Wesley puts it as a principle that God makes no difference between good and bad in the course of his providence, which would banish prayer out of the world by making it useless to men.

Gill alone refuses the indictment outright, and on both counts: it does not appear that Job had uttered anything vain enough to deserve comparison with the wind, and the fear meant here is the grace of fear, which is not what a man has by the light of nature and may cast off as Pharaoh did, but a blessing of the covenant of grace, sure and firm, and a part of internal grace that can never be lost. On the tongue of the crafty Clarke hears the old serpent who was subtle beyond all the beasts of the field, and concludes that such wisdom is not from above but from beneath. When Eliphaz closes by saying that Job's own mouth condemns him, Gill agrees that the mouth is judge and jury both, bringing in the verdict and standing instead of a thousand witnesses; Henry grants the force of it and then enters the objection nobody else enters, that the friends had provoked Job into saying what they now take advantage of, and that was not fair.
7:
Eliphaz now asks whether Job was the first man born, or made before the hills, and the voices take the sarcasm at its own measure. Clarke renders it as whether Job was born before Adam, and answers that it does not become the fallen descendant of a fallen parent to talk as Job does. Gill adds that the first Adam, created in wisdom, lost much of what he had by seeking more, and that unlawfully. Keil and Delitzsch supply the assumption behind the question, that the first created man, coming direct from the hand of God, had the profoundest insight into the mysteries of a world that came into being with him,. Henry turns the question into an argument: Adam suffered for sin, so will Job, who is so great a sufferer, not own himself a sinner? Ellicott alone treats it as a debating move, a retort upon the chapter where Job had claimed knowledge even for the inanimate creation. On the appeal to grey hairs that follows, Clarke notes that Eliphaz means himself and his two companions rather than the elders of their tribes, being the eldest of the three and so taking the lead in each part of the poem, while Henry hears the oldest of all claims, that all the ancient doctors are of our opinion, and answers that the oldest are not always the wisest.

The verse about the consolations of God is the chapter's obscurest, and two commentators say so at length rather than settle it. Clarke lays out eight renderings, from the Vulgate asking whether it can be a hard thing for God to comfort Job, through the Septuagint making him lightly scourged and immoderately spoken, to Coverdale and the Chaldee, remarks that scarcely any two translators agree even on the meaning, offers the Hebrew with a literal version, and leaves the reader to choose. Ellicott calls it very difficult to decide, allows that the common rendering gives good sense and suits the next verse, and then lists three other possibilities, one of which turns the second clause into the question whether Job's own speech was gentle. Keil and Delitzsch simply decide: the consolations are the promises made in accordance with the majesty and will of God, presupposing a humble resignation to His hand, and the word spoken in gentleness is the mild tone the friends had kept while Job passionately opposed them. Wesley reads it the same way, as the comforts they had held out on condition of repentance. Henry takes the charge as a slight put on divine consolations in general, and draws from it the observation that we are apt to think great and considerable what we ourselves say, when others with good reason think it small.

The last two verses accuse Job of being carried away and of turning his spirit against God. Clarke gives the winking eye two readings, the sparkle excited by pleasing objects or the furious rolling observed in deranged persons, prefers a rendering that asks whither Job's soul hurries him and what his rolling eyes mean, and concludes that none but a madman could speak and act so. Keil and Delitzsch are blunter still, rendering the clause as turning his snorting against God. Gill, who elsewhere defends Job, concedes only that a deceitful heart sometimes carries away even good men, and that if in any instance this was Job's case it was owing to his own heart. Henry grants the distinction that matters, that it was bad for the heart to be carried away from God but much worse for it to be turned against Him, and then says what no one else will say: Eliphaz wanted candour and charity, and to construe a tempted man's words this way was in effect to give the cause on Satan's side and to own that Job had done what Satan said he would.
14:
Eliphaz now falls back on a doctrine rather than a charge, and the voices first establish how low the words put man. Clarke takes the noun to mean what is weak, sickly, dying and miserable, and Gill, who renders it woeful man after Mr. Broughton, says the question is put by way of contempt, to abate any high conceit a man has of himself, since he is not naturally clean, cannot make himself so, and may be clean in his own eyes or his neighbours' while he is not clean in the sight of God. Ellicott notes only that this is the ceaseless burden of the book, returned to again and again. Henry alone presses the use being made of it. The truths are plain enough, that righteousness is cleanness and that man in his fallen state cannot pretend to acquit himself before God's justice; but Job had said the very same thing two chapters earlier, asking who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean. Does it follow that Job is the hypocrite he denies being? By no means. Though man as born of a woman is not clean, yet as born again of the Spirit he is clean.

On the next verse, that God puts no trust in His holy ones and that the heavens are not clean in His sight, the question is whom they denote. Wesley takes them for the angels, who though created holy fell in great numbers, and the heavens for the angels that dwell there, concluding that they are pure from corruption but not from imperfection. Clarke agrees, citing the Vulgate for the sense that among His saints none is immutable and Coverdale for unfaithfulness found among His own; nothing is immutable but God, so that saints may fall and angels may fall, all their goodness being derived and dependent. Gill takes them for sanctified men, chosen and set apart by grace, and makes the point that God trusts them with much, the prophets with His messages and ministers with a treasure in earthen vessels, yet trusts none of them with themselves, having put their regeneration and preservation into the hands of His Son and Spirit. Henry allows both and keeps the comparative force: God employs either sort but confides in neither without fresh supplies of strength, and if the stars have no light in the sight of the sun, what light has the sun in the sight of God?

The verse that follows is the one place in the chapter where a commentator proposes to reverse the reading. Clarke argues that since the previous line says God puts no trust in His holy ones, the particle should be rendered how much less, not how much more: how much less would He put confidence in man. Henry, working from the received text, arrives at the same sense by another road, that if saints are not to be trusted much less sinners, and if the heavens are not pure, which are as God made them, much less man, who is degenerated. On the closing image all four agree and differ only in illustration. Clarke has a man under sinful propensities drinking sin as greedily as a thirsty man or a camel drinks water, and sets the finished character of a bad man, who hungers and thirsts after sin, against the good man whose appetite is for righteousness. Wesley makes it habit added to proneness, swallowed as freely as men do in those hot countries. Henry says it gratifies without satisfying, like water to a man in a dropsy, so that the more men sin the more they would sin. Ellicott observes what the generality is for: language this strong, couched in general terms, is doubtless meant to reflect on Job, or it would not have needed to be so strong.
17:
Eliphaz turns from reproof to proof, and the voices agree on what he undertakes to prove. Gill states the thesis plainly: only wicked men and not righteous men are afflicted of God, and especially not in the manner Job was. Wesley has him say it in the first person, that such strokes as Job's are peculiar to hypocrites, and that he speaks not by hearsay but from his own experience. Keil and Delitzsch mark the change of ground: in his first speech the dogma came to him by a revelation, and here it rests on what he has himself observed and on reliable tradition, the verb for seeing being used of ordinary sight rather than of ecstatic vision. Ellicott notices that the second ground is not even his own, since in appealing to what wise men have handed down from their fathers he adopts the language his companion had used, and sets the whole appeal in an age prior to civil commotion and foreign disturbance.

Henry fastens on the preface itself. Eliphaz promises to show Job something worth hearing, and not unprofitable talk such as Job's; so apt are men, when they condemn the reasonings of others, to commend their own. But Henry will not let the method be discredited by the man using it. Taking notice of the providences of God toward the children of men is of good use, and many a lesson may be learned from them, and we may speak boldly when we declare what we have seen. The second ground he defends as warmly: the wisdom of the moderns is very much derived from that of the ancients, and what we have received from our ancestors we must transmit and not hide from the generations to come, for if the thread of the knowledge of many ages is cut off by the carelessness of one, all who succeed fare the worse.

Who these authorities were is disputed. Clarke takes them for the Israelites, who received possession of the promised land from God himself with no stranger permitted to dwell in it, mentions that some prefer Noah and his sons, and holds that, system apart, the words fit the Israelites better. Gill argues the other way, that the clause cannot be restrained to Canaan and the patriarchs, who very probably did not yet enjoy it, and that larger tracts and an earlier time are meant, most likely Noah and his sons, to whom the whole earth was given and among whom it was divided. Henry grants that the dictates of wisdom come with advantage from those in places of dignity and power, as from Solomon, and then sets a limit to the whole appeal: there is a wisdom which none of the princes of this world knew.

The sting is in the phrase about the stranger who never passed among them, and two voices draw it out. Job had said that the earth is given into the hand of the wicked; Eliphaz answers that it was given to these favoured men alone, and that no stranger came through to disturb or despoil them. Wesley makes the application explicit and merciless: no enemy could invade those holy men because God watched over them, and so He would have watched over Job, had Job been such a one, instead of leaving him to the Sabeans and the Chaldeans. Henry hears the same taunt and answers it with the one distinction that undoes the argument: many of God's people have indeed prospered in this world, as the patriarchs did, but it does not follow that those who are crossed and impoverished, as Job is, are therefore not God's people. Clarke's verdict on everything that follows is of a piece with that. Eliphaz is about to quote a whole collection of wise sayings from the ancients, all good enough in themselves, but sinfully misapplied to the case before him.
20:
The picture of the wicked man's misery opens on his inward state, and the readings differ in strength. Clarke puts it bluntly, that a life of sin is a life of misery and he who will sin must suffer, and takes the verb to mean that the man torments himself, a true self-tormentor who alone is the author of his own ruin. Keil and Delitzsch render it that he writhes, suffering inward distress so long as he lives, with numbered years reserved for the tyrant. Ellicott corrects the division of the sentence, so that the pain lasts all his days, even the number of years laid up for the oppressor, rather than standing as two independent statements; and he judges the whole passage a highly-coloured and poetical description, true to the character of the speaker. Gill divides the pain between the labour of iniquity, the sorrows of keeping wealth that scratch like thorns, and the gripes of conscience, and adds the qualification the others omit, that this cannot be said of every wicked man. Wesley supplies the motive for naming the oppressor in particular: Eliphaz supposed Job guilty of that sin, and chose it in opposition to what Job had said about the safety of such men.

On the dreadful sound in his ears the voices supply different causes. Gill separates fears that are imaginary from fears that are real. A man may flee when none pursues, a terror to himself and to all about him, like the first murderer who feared that every man he met would slay him; or the sound may be an actual one, the alarm of war, or report following report of one calamity after another. He then turns the verse on the man it was aimed at, since this is how Job's own troubles reached him, by one messenger of bad tidings after another. Clarke has the oppressor full of suspicions that the cruelties he exercised on others will one day be exercised on himself, so that he cannot rest even in prosperity. Henry traces it all to the conscience, which astonishes and confounds a man with the thought of the blood in which he has imbrued his hands, so that he knows both heaven and earth are incensed against him; and since he who kills with the sword must be killed with the sword, a guilty conscience shows him a flaming sword turning every way and himself running upon it.

Two of the images provoke open disagreement. Gill reads the refusal to believe in a return out of darkness partly of the infidel who knows he must be laid in the dark and silent grave, without hope of a glorious resurrection. Clarke doubts that reading, holding that the doctrine of a future judgment was understood in every part of the East where the knowledge of the true God was diffused, and keeps the plainer sense, that if the man takes a few steps in the dark he expects the dagger of the assassin. On the wandering abroad for bread Ellicott finds the portrait inconsistent, since a marauder reduced to begging is not the same figure, unless forage as well as plunder is meant by the raids; Henry has no such difficulty, taking the man to be frightening himself with a poverty not yet arrived, and notes that he cannot dig, being too fat, while to beg he may well be ashamed. The last verse is read for force rather than sense. Clarke makes the man's life a mark for the meanest assassin, deserted and then slain by his own troops, quoting the poet that few usurpers go down to the shades by a dry death. Ellicott has calamity prevail over him like a king, leaving him the tennis-ball of misfortune. Henry asks the question that sums the passage up: what is the hell before him, if this be the hell within him?
25:
Here Eliphaz gives the reason for all the calamities he has described, and the voices measure the presumption. Wesley puts it shortest, that the madness of this poor worm is that he dared to fight the omnipotent God. Clarke keeps the figure political: while in power the man thought himself supreme, and used his power not to protect but to oppress those he ruled. Henry presses the absurdity, that God is out of the sinner's reach and yet he stretches out his hand, to show that if it were in his power he would ungod him; it is the prodigious madness of presumptuous sinners that they enter the lists with Omnipotence.

The next verse is the chapter's hardest crux, because the voices do not agree on who assails whom. Gill and Wesley take the wicked man for the assailant: he runs on with a stretched-out neck, as the he-goat of the prophet's vision ran upon the ram in the fury of his power, or as a stout warrior who comes close and grapples, striking even at the bosses where his adversary is strongest. Henry has the same reading and adds the futility, a desperate combatant who finds himself unequally matched and flies in his enemy's face though he falls on the sword's point. Clarke reverses the subject altogether, noting that Calmet rightly refers the clause to God, who like a mighty conquering hero marches against the ungodly, rushes upon him and seizes him by the throat, which the mail about it cannot protect. Ellicott keeps the wicked man as subject but reassigns the armour, holding it less probable that the shield is God's and more likely that it is the man's own prosperity, which has blinded and hardened him so that he thinks himself fully covered against the vengeance of the Most High.

On the fatness that covers his face the readings are complementary rather than rival. Clarke sees a man overloaded with flesh who cannot defend himself against the strong gripe of an adversary, and reports that where the Hebrew speaks of collops of fat on the flanks the Arabic has a proverb about laying the Pleiades upon the Hyades, meaning an ambition without bounds, like the old giants piling one mountain on another to scale heaven; a haughty spirit goes before a fall, and such men's heaven is reduced to a chaos. Henry gets two things from the one image: the fat on the face makes a man look bold and haughty, and the fat on the flanks makes him lie easy and feel little, but it will prove poor shelter against the darts of God's wrath.

The desolate cities he inhabits are read four ways. Gill and Henry make them his own ruins, cities he destroyed and then rebuilt greater to perpetuate his name, or emptied of their inhabitants that he might be placed alone in them, proud and cruel men taking a strange pleasure in ruins of their own making. Clarke makes the ruins his punishment instead, since it is sometimes a tyrant's fate to be obliged to lodge in a city his own wars had wrecked. Keil and Delitzsch deny that they are his ruins at all, on the ground that the verb points to a divinely appointed future and that an appeal to the law forbidding the rebuilding of accursed cities is out of place in this book, since dwelling and not rebuilding is what the verse mentions; they read it more generally, of a powerful man settling down carelessly without any fear of the judgments of God. Ellicott leaves the three possibilities open. Of the sentence that follows Clarke counts out six threatened evils and says plainly that the whole of it is directed against Job, whom Eliphaz indirectly accuses of having been a tyrant.
31:
The warning against trusting vanity is taken by every voice as general counsel, not another blow at Job. Gill traces the deceiving to Satan, to a man's own heart, and to the deceitfulness of sin, which promises profit, pleasure and liberty and issues in ruin, pain and bondage. Clarke puts it in one stroke: the man finds he has trusted in a lie, and this lie is his recompense. Wesley hears a caution to all men not to run into the same error, and reads the recompense as an exchange, one vanity for another, a pleasing vanity for a vexatious one. Henry says the same with the figure that fits it: let the mischiefs that befall others be our warnings, and let us not rest on that broken reed which always failed those who leaned on it, for such men sow the wind and reap the whirlwind.

On the untimely end that follows, Gill makes a distinction the others pass over. The man's days are cut short not before the time fixed in the decree and purpose of God, but before his own time, the term his healthy constitution seemed to promise. Clarke prefers the Vulgate's plainer sense, that he shall perish before his days are completed, and takes it of a violent death and of a stock from which no scion grows. The voices divide the loss between a man's goods and his children. Gill allows both, a vine shaken by tempest and stripped of its unripe grapes, and adds that respect is perhaps had to Job's case in his substance and his family alike. Clarke takes it of the children only, windfall grapes and blasted olive blossoms,, the oppressor's hopeful progeny falling without ever realising what was expected of them. Henry has them shaken off as blossoms that never knit, and draws the general rule that many a man's family is ruined by his iniquity.

The word for desolate in the next verse catches three voices at once, and one of them sees what is being done with it. Ellicott notes that this was Job's own word, used by him earlier, and that since it is an uncommon one there may be an intentional reference to his use of it. Keil and Delitzsch make the family-circle of the ungodly a hard, lifeless, stony mass, stark dead. What the verse insinuates neither Gill nor Clarke will leave unsaid. Gill thinks Eliphaz has his eye on Job's own household, representing its head, his children and his servants as all hypocrites and now made desolate. Clarke says flatly that Job is here classed with hypocrites, and that the clause about bribery is a second insinuation, that he had perverted justice and taken bribes.

The last verse returns to the figure of conception and birth: the wicked conceive mischief from the seed Satan sows in their hearts, travail with many pangs, and bring forth deception. Keil and Delitzsch put the recoil in a sentence, that they hatch sorrow for others and what comes of it is evil for themselves. Henry names the two ingredients as malice and falsehood, the stock in trade of him who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning. Ellicott's verdict on the whole peroration is the sharpest thing said about it: the speaker only repeats the orthodox and familiar maxim that the wicked are punished in this life and the good by implication rewarded, a maxim which fails utterly in the face of afflictions like Job's, unless, as his friends insinuated, he was one of the wicked. Clarke ends where that leaves the sufferer, with a body wasted by disease, a mind harassed by Satan and a heart wrung by the false accusations of his friends, so that it is no wonder he was agitated and sometimes thrown off his guard; yet all his enemies were chained, and beyond that chain they could not go.
